entries.en: Under the Han it was a post kept close to the throne.
entries.literal: In Han times it was an intimate post at court.

entries.zh: 魏、晉選用，稍增華重，而大意不異。
entries.en: Wei and Jin made the appointment somewhat grander, yet its heart stayed the same.
entries.literal: Under Wei and Jin selection it gained a little more splendor and weight, but the essential character did not change.

entries.zh: 宋文帝元嘉中，王華、王曇首、殷景仁等，竝爲侍中，情在親密，與帝接膝共語，貂拂帝手，拔貂置案上，語畢復手插之。
entries.en: In Emperor Wen of Song's Yuanjia years Wang Hua, Wang Tan-shou, Yin Jingren, and others served together as gentlemen-in-attendance, intimate enough to talk knee to knee with the emperor—brushing his hand with their sable, slipping it off to lay on the table, then, when words were spent, sliding their hands back in.
entries.literal: In the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of Song, Wang Hua, Wang Tan-shou, Yin Jingren, and others all served as gentlemen-in-attendance; close in feeling, they spoke with the emperor knee to knee, brushed the imperial hand with their sable, drew the sable off and laid it on the table, and when speech was done slipped their hands back in.

entries.zh: 孝武時，侍中何偃南郊陪乘，鑾輅過白門閫，偃將匐，帝乃接之曰：「朕乃陪卿。」
entries.en: Under Emperor Xiaowu, He Yan, gentleman-in-attendance, rode beside the emperor at the southern suburb; as the train passed the White Gate barbican he was about to bow flat, and the emperor stayed him: "I shall keep you company."
entries.literal: In the Xiaowu era the gentleman-in-attendance He Yan rode beside the emperor at the southern suburb; when the imperial carriage passed the White Gate barbican Yan was about to prostrate himself, and the emperor caught him up, saying, "I shall accompany you."

entries.zh: 齊世朝會，多以美姿容者兼官。
entries.en: In Qi, court levees often doubled handsome men in other offices.
entries.literal: In Qi, court assemblies often gave concurrent posts to men of handsome bearing.

entries.zh: 永元三年，東昏南郊，不欲親朝士，以主璽陪乘，前代未嘗有也。
entries.en: In Yongyuan's third year Emperor Donghun, going to the southern suburb, refused to face the court gentlemen and set the keeper of the imperial seal beside him in the carriage—a thing no age before had seen.
entries.literal: In the third year of Yongyuan, when Emperor Donghun went to the southern suburb he would not face the court gentlemen and had the Keeper of the Imperial Seal ride beside him—something no earlier age had done.

entries.zh: 侍中呼爲門下。
entries.en: In court speech they were called "Gate Below."
entries.literal: The gentlemen-in-attendance were called "Gate Below."

entries.zh: 亦置令史。
entries.en: Clerk-recorders were appointed as well.
entries.literal: Clerk-recorders were also appointed.

entries.zh: 領官如左：
entries.en: It oversaw the following posts:
entries.literal: Subordinate offices are as follows:

entries.zh: 魏、晉世州牧隆重，刺史任重者爲使持節都督，輕者爲持節督，起漢從帝時，御史中丞馮赦討九江賊，督揚、徐二州軍事，而何、徐《宋志》云起魏武遣諸州將督軍，王珪之《職儀》云起光武，竝非也。
entries.en: Under Wei and Jin, provincial governors were honored posts; inspectors with heavy responsibility became commissioners bearing the staff of authority and military overseers, lighter ones commissioners bearing the staff and supervisors. The office began under Emperor Shun of Han, when Censor-in-chief Feng She campaigned against Jiujiang bandits and directed Yang and Xu military affairs; but He and Xu's Song Treatise dates it to Cao Cao's dispatch of provincial generals to oversee troops, and Wang Guizhi's Protocol of Offices dates it to Emperor Guangwu—all are mistaken.
entries.literal: In Wei and Jin times provincial governors were weighty; inspectors with heavy duty became commissioners bearing the staff of authority and overseers, lighter ones commissioners bearing the staff of authority and supervisors. It began in the time of Emperor Shun of Han, when Censor-in-chief Feng She suppressed bandits in Jiujiang and oversaw military affairs in Yang and Xu provinces; yet He and Xu's Song Treatise says it began when Cao Cao sent generals of the provinces to oversee armies, and Wang Guizhi's Protocol of Offices says it began with Guangwu—all are wrong.

entries.zh: 晉太康中，都督知軍事，刺史治民，各用人。
entries.en: In Jin Taikang the military overseer commanded troops and the inspector governed the people, each with separate staffs.
entries.literal: In Jin Taikang, the overseer handled military affairs and the inspector governed the people; each had his own appointees.

entries.zh: 惠帝末，乃幷任，非要州則單爲刺史。
entries.en: By the end of Emperor Hui the two offices were combined; save in a vital province, a man held the inspectorate alone.
entries.literal: At the end of Emperor Hui's reign the two posts were merged; unless it was a key province, one person alone served as regional inspector.

entries.zh: 州朝置別駕、治中、議曹、文學祭酒、諸曹部從事史。
entries.en: At every provincial court stood a chief administrator, a registrar, a deliberation bureau, a libationer of letters and learning, and the section clerks of the various departments.
entries.literal: Each province had a chief administrator, registrar, deliberation office, libationer of letters and literature, and section clerks for the various departments.

entries.zh: 南齊書卷十六‧志第八百官
entries.en: Volume 16 Treatises 8: Official Posts
entries.literal: Book of Southern Qi, Volume 16 — Treatise 8: Hundred Officials

entries.zh: 昔三皇乘祇車出谷口，夏氏以奚仲爲車正，殷有瑞車，山車垂句是也。
entries.en: In antiquity the Three Sovereigns rode the sacred carriage out from the valley gate; the Xia appointed Xi Zhong Master of Chariots; the Yin had the auspicious chariot — the mountain cart with drooping axles tells that tale.
entries.literal: In antiquity the Three Sovereigns rode the spirit carriage out from the valley mouth; the Xia made Xi Zhong Master of Chariots; the Yin had the auspicious carriage — the mountain carriage with drooping axles is meant.

entries.zh: 《周禮》匠人爲輿，以象天地。
entries.en: The Rites of Zhou have the craftsman shape the carriage as Heaven and Earth in miniature.
entries.literal: In the Rites of Zhou the craftsman builds the carriage to symbolize Heaven and Earth.

entries.zh: 漢武天漢四年，朝諸侯甘泉宮，定輿服制，班于天下。
entries.en: In Han Wudi's Tianhan 4 he assembled the feudal lords at Sweet Springs Palace, set the carriage and regalia code, and sent it throughout the empire.
entries.literal: In Tianhan year 4 of Han Wudi, he convened the feudal lords at Sweet Springs Palace, fixed the carriage-and-dress code, and promulgated it throughout the realm.

entries.zh: 光武建武十三年，得公孫述葆車，輿輦始具。
entries.en: In Guangwu's Jianwu 13 he captured Gongsun Shu's treasure carriage; the full set of state litters was first assembled.
entries.literal: In Jianwu year 13 Guangwu obtained Gongsun Shu's treasure carriage; litters and palanquins were first complete.

entries.zh: 蔡邕創立此志，馬彪勒成漢典，晉摯虞治禮，亦議五輅制度。
entries.en: Cai Yong began this treatise; Ma Biao finished the Han record; under Jin, Zhi Yu curated the rites and debated the five ceremonial chariots as well.
entries.literal: Cai Yong founded this treatise; Ma Biao compiled the Han canon; Jin's Zhi Yu curated the rites and likewise debated the system of the Five Regalia Chariots.

entries.zh: 江左之始，車服多闕，但有金戎，省充庭之儀。
entries.en: Early in the southeast court, carriages and dress were mostly missing; only the golden war carriage survived, and the palace-yard display was cut back.
entries.literal: At the beginning of the southeastern court, carriages and dress were largely lacking; only the golden war carriage remained, and the hall-filling ceremony was reduced.

entries.zh: 太興中，太子臨學，無高蓋車，元帝詔乘安車。
entries.en: In Taixing, when the crown prince went to his studies there was no high-canopy coach; Yuan Di ordered him to use the comfort carriage instead.
entries.literal: In the Taixing era, when the crown prince attended school there was no high-canopy carriage; Emperor Yuan decreed that he ride the comfort carriage.

entries.zh: 元、明時，屬車唯九乘。
entries.en: Under Emperors Yuan and Ming, the train had only nine following carriages.
entries.literal: In the Yuan and Ming reigns, the following carriages numbered only nine.

entries.zh: 永和中，石虎死後，舊工人奔叛歸國，稍造車輿。
entries.en: In Yonghe, after Shi Hu died, old artisans fled home and chariot-making slowly resumed.
entries.literal: In the Yonghe era, after Shi Hu's death, veteran craftsmen deserted and returned to the state; chariots were gradually made again.

entries.zh: 太元中，苻堅敗後，又得偽車輦，於是屬車增爲十二乘。
entries.en: In Taiyuan, after Fu Jian's defeat they seized Former Qin litters and raised the train to twelve carriages.
entries.literal: In the Taiyuan era, after Fu Jian's defeat, they again obtained the Former Qin litters; then the following carriages increased to twelve.

entries.zh: 義熙中，宋武平關、洛，得姚興偽車輦。
entries.en: In Yixi, Emperor Wu of Song took the Pass and Luoyang and captured Yao Xing's Qin litters.
entries.literal: In the Yixi era Song Wu pacified the Pass and Luoyang and obtained Yao Xing's Former Qin litters.

entries.zh: 宋大明改脩輦輅，妙盡時華，始備偽氐，復設充庭之制。
entries.en: Under Song's Daming they rebuilt the litters and ceremonial chariots with every luxury of the age, first completed the Qin equipment, and restored the palace-yard display.
entries.literal: In Song's Daming era they renovated the litters and regalia chariots, exhaustingly refined in contemporary splendor; they first completed the Qin set and restored the hall-filling institution.

entries.zh: 永明中，更增藻飾，盛於前矣。
entries.en: In Yongming they added still richer ornament — grander than ever.
entries.literal: In the Yongming era they further added ornamental refinement, surpassing what came before.

entries.zh: 案《周禮》以檢《漢志》，名器不同，晉、宋改革，稍與世異，今記時事而已。
entries.en: Measured against the Rites of Zhou and the Han Treatise, titles and regalia no longer match; Jin and Song revisions drifted from ancient usage — here only the present is recorded.
entries.literal: Checking the Rites of Zhou against the Han Treatise, the names and vessels differ; Jin and Song reforms diverged somewhat from the age; this record sets down present affairs only.

entries.zh: 五輅，江左相承駕四馬，左右騑爲六。
entries.en: The Five Regalia Chariots: in the southeast court they were routinely drawn by four horses, with left and right outriders making six in all.
entries.literal: The Five Regalia Chariots: south of the Yangtze they successively used four horses to draw them, with left and right outriders making six.

entries.zh: 施絳系游御繩，其重轂貳轄飛軨幡，用赤油令，有紫真毦。
entries.en: Crimson touring reins were fitted; double hubs, paired linchpins, flying nave pennants followed the red-oil rule, with purple true down.
entries.literal: Crimson cord touring reins were fitted; their double hubs, paired linchpins, flying naves, and pennants used the red-oil decree, with purple true down.

entries.zh: 左纛，置左騑馬軛上。
entries.en: The left great banner was fixed to the left outrider's yoke.
entries.literal: The left great banner was set on the yoke of the left outrider horse.

entries.zh: 金鍐，金加冠，狀如玉華形，在馬鍐上。
entries.en: The golden cheek-piece: gold crowned in a jade-flower shape, mounted on the horse's cheek-piece.
entries.literal: The golden cheek-piece — gold added to the crown, shaped like the jade-flower form, set on the horse's cheek-piece.

entries.zh: 方釳，鐵廣數寸，有三孔，插翟尾其中。
entries.en: The square iron plate, several inches across, with three holes to take pheasant tails.
entries.literal: The square iron plate, several inches wide, with three holes for inserting pheasant tails.

entries.zh: 繁纓，金塗紫皮，紫真毦，橫在馬膺前。
entries.en: The full tassel-crown: gold-plated purple leather and purple true down, laid crosswise before the horse's breast.
entries.literal: The full tassel-crown: gold-plated purple leather and purple true down, set crosswise before the horse's breast.

entries.zh: 鏤鍚，刻金爲馬面當顱。
entries.en: The carved golden brow: gold chased into the horse's forehead plate.
entries.literal: The carved golden brow: gold chased as the horse's forehead plate.

entries.zh: 皆如古制。
entries.en: All followed the ancient pattern.
entries.literal: All followed the ancient institution.

entries.zh: 世祖永明初，加玉輅爲重蓋，又作麒麟頭，采畫，以馬首戴之。
entries.en: Early in Yongming, Emperor Shizu gave the Jade Regalia Chariot a double canopy and fashioned a painted qilin head for the horses to wear.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Yongming, Emperor Shizu added a double canopy to the jade regalia carriage and also made a qilin head, painted in colors, to be worn on the horse's head.

entries.zh: 竟陵王子良啓曰：「臣聞車旗有章，載自前史，器必依禮，服無舛法。
entries.en: Prince Ziliang of Jingling submitted: "I have heard that carriage banners have their statutes, set down in earlier histories; regalia must follow ritual, and dress must not break the code.
entries.literal: Prince Ziliang of Jingling submitted: "I have heard that carriage banners have their regulations, recorded from former histories; vessels must follow ritual, and dress must not violate law.

entries.zh: 凡蓋員象天，軫方法地，上無二天之儀，下設兩蓋之飾，求之志錄，恐爲乖衷。
entries.en: The canopy is round as Heaven; the naves square as Earth. Above there is no rite of two heavens; below you add a double-canopy ornament — checked against the ritual records, I fear it misses the mark.
entries.literal: The canopy is round to symbolize Heaven; the naves square to symbolize Earth. Above there is no rite of two Heavens; below you set the ornament of two canopies — sought in the ritual records, I fear this is contrary to the intent.

entries.zh: 又假爲麟首，加乎馬頭，事不師古，鮮或可施。」
entries.en: Again you set a false qilin head on the horses; the thing does not follow antiquity — it can hardly be allowed."
entries.literal: Again you falsely make a qilin head and set it on the horse's head; the matter does not take the ancients as teacher — scarcely can it be applied."

entries.zh: 建武中，明帝乃省重蓋等。
entries.en: In the Jianwu era, Emperor Ming abolished the double canopy and similar additions.
entries.literal: In the Jianwu era, Emperor Ming then abolished the double canopy and the like.

entries.zh: 宋昇明三年，錫齊王大輅、戎輅各一。
entries.en: In Song Shengming 3 the court bestowed on the King of Qi one great chariot and one war chariot.
entries.literal: In Shengming year 3 of Song, one great chariot and one war chariot each were bestowed on the King of Qi.

entries.zh: 乘黃五輅，無大輅、戎輅。
entries.en: The Director of Carriages’ five chariots included no great chariot or war chariot.
entries.literal: The five chariots under the Director of Carriages had no great chariot or war chariot.

entries.zh: 左丞王逡之議：「大輅，殷之祭車，故不登周輅之名，而《明堂位》云『大輅，殷輅也』。
entries.en: Left Assistant Grandee Wang Qunzhi argued: "The great chariot was Yin’s sacrificial carriage, which is why it is absent from the Zhou chariot roster—yet the Hall of Brightness states, 'The great chariot is the Yin chariot.'
entries.literal: Left Assistant Grandee Wang Qunzhi argued: "The great chariot was Yin’s sacrificial carriage; therefore it does not appear among the Zhou chariot names. Yet the Hall of Brightness says 'The great chariot is the Yin chariot.'

entries.zh: 注云『大輅，木輅也』。
entries.en: The commentary reads: 'The great chariot is the wood chariot.'
entries.literal: The comment says 'The great chariot is the wood chariot.'

entries.zh: 《月令》『中央土，乘大輅』。
entries.en: The Monthly Ordinances: 'At the center, earth—ride the great chariot.'
entries.literal: The Monthly Ordinances: 'In the center, earth—ride the great chariot.'

entries.zh: 注云『殷輅也』。
entries.en: The commentary: 'The Yin chariot.'
entries.literal: The comment says 'The Yin chariot.'

entries.zh: 《禮器》『大輅繁纓一就』。
entries.en: Ritual Vessels: 'The great chariot—plaited tassels in one set.'
entries.literal: Ritual Vessels: 'The great chariot—plaited tassels, one set.'

entries.zh: 注云『大輅，殷之祭天車也』。
entries.en: The commentary: 'The great chariot is Yin’s carriage for sacrificing to Heaven.'
entries.literal: The comment says 'The great chariot is Yin’s carriage for sacrificing to Heaven.'

entries.zh: 《周禮》五路，玉路、金路、象路、革路、木路。
entries.en: The Rites of Zhou names five paths: jade, gold, ivory, leather, and wood.
entries.literal: The Rites of Zhou lists five paths: jade path, gold path, ivory path, leather path, and wood path.

entries.zh: 則周之木輅，殷之大路也。
entries.en: Zhou’s wood chariot, then, is Yin’s great chariot.
entries.literal: Thus Zhou’s wood chariot is Yin’s great chariot.

entries.zh: 周革路建大白，以卽戎，此則戎路也。
entries.en: Zhou’s leather path raises the great white standard for war—this is the war path.
entries.literal: Zhou’s leather path raises the great white [banner] to go to war—this is the war path.

entries.zh: 意謂國之大事，在祀與戎，故錫以殷祭天之車，與周之卽戎之路。
entries.en: The point is that a state’s weightiest business is sacrifice and war—hence the grant of Yin’s Heaven-sacrificing carriage together with Zhou’s war chariot.
entries.literal: The reasoning is that the great affairs of state lie in sacrifice and war; therefore they were granted Yin’s Heaven-sacrificing carriage and Zhou’s war-going path.

entries.zh: 祀則以殷，戎必以周者，明郊天義遠，建前代之禮，卽戎事近，故以今世之制。
entries.en: Sacrifice follows Yin; war must follow Zhou—because suburban Heaven worship looks far back and installs an earlier dynasty’s rite, whereas military affairs are immediate and call for the current house’s forms.
entries.literal: For sacrifice use Yin; for war necessarily use Zhou—showing that suburban Heaven rites are remote in meaning and establish a prior age’s ritual, while military matters are near, so the present dynasty’s regulation applies.

entries.zh: 《明堂位》云『魯君孟春乘大路，載十有二旒日月之章，祀帝于郊』。
entries.en: The Hall of Brightness says: 'In mid-spring the lord of Lu rides the great road chariot, with twelve sun-and-moon streamers, and sacrifices to the Thearch in the suburbs.'
entries.literal: The Hall of Brightness says 'In mid-spring the lord of Lu rides the great road [chariot], bearing twelve streamers with sun-and-moon emblems, sacrificing to the Thearch in the suburbs.'

entries.zh: 天必以大輅以錫諸侯，良有以也。
entries.en: That Heaven should bestow the great chariot on feudal lords is entirely reasonable.
entries.literal: That Heaven must bestow the great chariot upon feudal lords is well founded indeed.

entries.zh: 今木路，卽大路也。」
entries.en: Today’s wood path is precisely that great road chariot."
entries.literal: Now the wood path is precisely the great road [chariot]."

entries.zh: 太尉左長史王儉議，宜用金輅九旒。
entries.en: Grand Marshal’s left chief clerk Wang Jian proposed the gold chariot with nine streamers.
entries.literal: Grand Marshal’s left chief clerk Wang Jian argued that the gold chariot with nine streamers should be used.

entries.zh: 時乘黃無副，借用五輅，大朝臨軒，權列三輅。
entries.en: The Director of Carriages then had no deputy, so the five chariots were borrowed; at great court before the throne hall three chariots were set out provisionally.
entries.literal: At the time the Director of Carriages had no deputy; they borrowed the five chariots—for great court at the throne hall they provisionally arrayed three chariots.

entries.zh: 《虞書》曰：「予欲觀古人之象，日、月、星辰、山、龍、華蟲作繢，宗彝、藻、火、粉米、黼、黻絺繡，以五采章施于五色。」
entries.en: The Book of Yu says: "I wish to view the images of antiquity—sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and patterned creatures embroidered; ancestral vessels, algae, fire, rice powder, fu and fu in fine silk, with the five colors displayed on the five hues."
entries.literal: The Book of Yu says: "I wish to view the images of antiquity—sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and patterned creatures embroidered; ancestral vessels, algae, fire, rice powder, fu and fu in fine silk, with the five colors displayed on the five hues."

entries.zh: 天子服備日、月以下，公山、龍以下，侯伯華蟲以下，子男藻、火以下，卿大夫粉米以下。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven's robes bore the sun and moon and all below them; a duke bore mountains and dragons and below; a marquis or earl bore patterned creatures and below; a viscount or baron bore algae and fire and below; ministers and grandees bore rice powder and below.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven's dress included the sun and moon and below; the duke mountains and dragons and below; marquis and earl patterned creatures and below; viscount and baron algae and fire and below; ministers and grandees rice powder and below.

entries.zh: 天子六冕，王后六服，著在周官。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven had six crowns and the empress six garments, as set forth in the Offices of Zhou.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven had six crowns and the empress six garments, set forth in the Offices of Zhou.

entries.zh: 公侯以下，咸有名則，佩玉組綬，竝具禮文，後代沿革，見《漢志晉服制令》，其冠十三品，見蔡邕《獨斷》，竝不復具詳。
entries.en: Below duke and marquis every rank had named rules for jade pendants and cord sashes, all spelled out in ritual texts; later changes appear in the Han Treatise and Jin dress regulations, and the thirteen crown grades in Cai Yong's Duduan—not repeated here.
entries.literal: Below duke and marquis all had named regulations, jade pendants and cord sashes, all fully specified in ritual texts; later changes appear in the Han Treatise and Jin dress regulations—the thirteen crown grades appear in Cai Yong's Duduan; they are not detailed here.

entries.zh: 宋明帝泰始四年，更制五輅，議脩五冕，朝會饗獵，各有所服，事見《宋注》。
entries.en: In the fourth year of Taishi, Emperor Ming of Song revised the five regalia chariots and debated restoring the five crowns; court assembly, feasts, and hunts each had its own dress, as recorded in the Song commentaries.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Taishi, Emperor Ming of Song revised the five regalia chariots and deliberated restoring the five crowns; court assembly, feasts, and hunts each had its own dress—the matter appears in the Song commentaries.

entries.zh: 舊相承三公以下冕七旒，青玉珠，卿大夫以下五旒，黑玉珠。
entries.en: By long practice, ranks below the three excellencies wore crowns of seven tassels with blue jade beads; ministers and grandees wore five tassels with black jade beads.
entries.literal: By long-standing practice, below the three excellencies the crown had seven tassels with blue jade beads; below ministers and grandees, five tassels with black jade beads.

entries.zh: 永明六年，太常丞何諲之議，案《周禮》命數，改三公八旒，卿六旒。
entries.en: In the sixth year of Yongming, Director of Rites Assistant He Yin-zhi proposed, on the Zhou Rites rank scheme, to raise the three excellencies to eight tassels and ministers to six.
entries.literal: In the sixth year of Yongming, Director of Rites Assistant He Yin-zhi proposed, following the Zhou Rites rank numbers, to change the three excellencies to eight tassels and ministers to six.

entries.zh: 尚書令王儉議，依漢三公服，山、龍九章，卿華蟲七章。
entries.en: Director of the Masters of Writing Wang Jian proposed following Han practice: nine sections of mountains and dragons for the three excellencies, seven sections of patterned creatures for ministers.
entries.literal: Director of the Masters of Writing Wang Jian proposed following Han dress for the three excellencies—mountains and dragons in nine sections—and for ministers, patterned creatures in seven sections.

entries.zh: 從之。
entries.en: The court adopted it.
entries.literal: The court adopted it.

entries.zh: 輦車，如犢車，竹蓬。
entries.en: The palanquin carriage resembled a calf cart, with a bamboo awning.
entries.literal: Palanquin carriage, like a calf cart, with bamboo awning.

entries.zh: 廂外鑿鏤金薄，碧紗衣，織成芚，錦衣。
entries.en: Outside the compartment were carved openwork gold leaf, green gauze garments, woven matting, and brocade clothing.
entries.literal: Outside the compartment, carved openwork gold leaf; green gauze garment; woven-pattern matting; brocade clothing.

entries.zh: 廂裏及仰頂隱膝後戶，金塗鏤面，瑇瑁帖，金塗松精，登仙花紐，綠四緣，四望紗萌子，上下前後眉，鏤鍱。
entries.en: Inside the compartment and on the upward-facing roof were the hidden knee and rear door, gilt openwork facing, tortoiseshell appliqué, gilt pine essence, ascending-immortal flower clasps, green four-border trim, a four-view gauze awning, brows front and back above and below, and openwork plaques.
entries.literal: Inside the compartment and on the upward-facing top, hidden knee and rear door; gilt openwork facing; tortoiseshell appliqué; gilt pine essence; ascending-immortal flower clasps; green four-border trim; four-view gauze awning; upper, lower, front, and rear brows; openwork plaques.

entries.zh: 轅枕長角龍，白牙蘭，瑇瑁金塗校飾。
entries.en: The shaft pillow bore a long-horned dragon, white ivory orchid, and tortoiseshell with gilt fittings.
entries.literal: Shaft pillow [with] long-horned dragon; white ivory orchid; tortoiseshell and gilt fittings.

entries.zh: 漆鄣塵板在蘭前，金銀花獸玃天龍師子鏤面，榆花鈿指子摩尼炎，金龍虎。
entries.en: Before the orchid stood a lacquer dust-screen board with openwork facing of gold and silver floral beasts, a heaven-reaching dragon, and lions; elm-flower inlay, finger-guards, mani flame, and gold dragon and tiger.
entries.literal: Lacquer dust-screen board before the orchid; gold and silver floral beasts, heaven-reaching dragon, lion openwork facing; elm-flower inlay, finger-guard, mani flame; gold dragon and tiger.

entries.zh: 扶轅，銀口帶，龍板頭。
entries.en: Shaft supports, silver mouth-bands, and dragon board heads.
entries.literal: Shaft supports; silver mouth-band; dragon board head.

entries.zh: 龍轅軛上，金鳳皇鈴璅，銀口帶，星後梢，瑇瑁帖，金塗香沓，銀星花獸幔竿杖，金塗龍牽，縱橫長，背花香染兆牀副。
entries.en: On the dragon shaft yoke were gilt phoenix bells and links, silver mouth-bands, star rear tips, tortoiseshell appliqué, gilt fragrant tread, silver star floral beast curtain-pole staffs, gilt dragon draws, lengthwise and crosswise long pieces, and a back floral incense-dyed omen-bed adjunct.
entries.literal: On the dragon shaft yoke, gilt phoenix bells and links; silver mouth-band; star rear tip; tortoiseshell appliqué; gilt fragrant tread; silver star floral beast curtain-pole staff; gilt dragon draw; lengthwise and crosswise long [pieces]; back floral incense-dyed omen bed adjunct.

entries.zh: 自輦以下，二宮御車，皆綠油幢，絳系絡。
entries.en: From the palanquin carriage downward, imperial carriages of the two palaces all bore green oil canopies and crimson cord netting.
entries.literal: From the palanquin downward, the two palaces' imperial carriages all had green oil canopies and crimson cord netting.

entries.zh: 御所乘，雙棟。
entries.en: The sovereign's carriage had double ridgepoles.
entries.literal: That which the sovereign rides has double ridgepoles.

entries.zh: 其公主則碧油幢云。
entries.en: Princesses, it is said, used the blue-green oil canopy.
entries.literal: For princesses it is the blue-green oil canopy, it is said.

entries.zh: 《司馬法》曰「夏后氏輦曰金車，殷曰胡奴車，周曰輜車」，皆輦也。
entries.en: The Methods of Sima says: "Under the Xia the palanquin was called the Golden Carriage; under Yin the Barbarian-Servant Carriage; under Zhou the Supply Carriage"—all names for the palanquin.
entries.literal: The Methods of Sima says, "Under the Xia the palanquin was called the Golden Carriage; under Yin the Barbarian-Servant Carriage; under Zhou the Supply Carriage"—all are palanquins.

entries.zh: 《漢書叔孫通傳》云「皇帝輦出房」，成帝輦過後宮，此朝宴竝用也。
entries.en: The Biography of Shusun Tong in the Book of Han says, "When the emperor's palanquin left the side chamber"; Emperor Cheng's palanquin passed through the rear palaces—court and banquet alike employed it.
entries.literal: The Biography of Shusun Tong in the Book of Han says, "When the emperor's palanquin left the side chamber"; Emperor Cheng's palanquin passed through the rear palaces—both court and banquet used it alike.

entries.zh: 《輿服志》云「輦車具金銀丹青采雘雕畫蒲陶之文，乘人以行」。
entries.en: The Treatise on Carriages and Dress says: "The palanquin carriage bore gold, silver, cinnabar, green, and polychrome carving with painted grapevine designs; bearers carried it forward."
entries.literal: The Treatise on Carriages and Dress says, "The palanquin carriage has gold, silver, cinnabar, green, and polychrome carving and painted grapevine designs; men carry it and it moves."

entries.zh: 信陽侯陰就見井丹，左右人進輦，是爲臣下亦得乘之。
entries.en: When Marquis Yin of Xinyang went to see Jing Dan, his attendants brought a palanquin—showing that even subjects might ride it.
entries.literal: Marquis Yin of Xinyang, when he went to see Jing Dan, had his attendants bring a palanquin—thus even subjects below the throne could ride it.

entries.zh: 晉武帝給安平獻王孚雲母輦。
entries.en: Emperor Wu of Jin granted Prince Xian of Anping, Sima Fu, a mica palanquin.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu of Jin granted Prince Xian of Anping, Fu, a mica palanquin.

entries.zh: 晉中朝又有香衣輦，江左唯御所乘。
entries.en: The Jin central court also had an incense-garment palanquin; east of the Yangtze only the sovereign rode it.
entries.literal: In the Jin central court there was also the incense-garment palanquin; east of the Yangtze only the sovereign rode it.

entries.zh: 南齊書卷十七‧志第九
entries.en: Volume 17 Treatises 9: Carriages and Dress
entries.literal: Book of Southern Qi, Volume 17 — Treatise 9

entries.zh: 永明中，蕭諶開博風帽後裙之制，爲破後帽。
entries.en: In Yongming, Xiao Chen introduced broad wind hats with long back skirts—the style called the torn-back hat.
entries.literal: During Yongming, Xiao Chen devised broad wind hats with trailing back skirts—the fashion called the torn-back hat.

entries.zh: 世祖崩後，諶建廢立，誅滅諸王。
entries.en: After Shizu’s death, Chen engineered deposition and enthronement and put the princes to death.
entries.literal: After Shizu’s death, Chen engineered deposition and enthronement and executed the princes.

entries.zh: 世祖起青溪舊宮，時人反之曰：「舊宮者，窮廄也。」
entries.en: Emperor Shizu restored the old palace at Qingxi; wits reversed the name and said "Old Palace—nothing but a beggared stable."
entries.literal: Emperor Shizu raised the old palace at Qingxi; people turned the name about and said "the Old Palace—that is a ruined stable."

entries.zh: 及上崩後，宮人出居之。
entries.en: When the emperor was gone, palace women were sent out to live there.
entries.literal: After the emperor died, palace women came out to dwell there.

entries.zh: 世祖起禪靈寺初成，百姓縱觀。
entries.en: When Emperor Shizu first completed Chanling Temple, the people thronged to see it.
entries.literal: When Emperor Shizu first finished the Chanling Temple, the people crowded to look.

entries.zh: 或曰：「禪者授也，靈非美名，所授必不得其人。」
entries.en: Some murmured: "Chan means to transmit; ling is no lucky word—whoever is handed the throne will not be fit to hold it."
entries.literal: Some said: "Chan means to hand on; ling is no fair name—whoever receives the charge will surely not be the right man."

entries.zh: 後太孫立，見廢也。
entries.en: Soon after the heir was enthroned—and cast down.
entries.literal: Later the heir apparent was set up and then deposed.

entries.zh: 永明中，宮內坐起御食之外，皆爲客食。
entries.en: In Yongming, inside the palace every meal but the emperor's own at morning and evening was called a guest meal.
entries.literal: In Yongming, within the palace, except for the emperor's own meals at sitting and rising, all were called guest meals.

entries.zh: 世祖以客非家人名，改呼爲別食，時人以爲分別之象。
entries.en: Emperor Shizu said guest was no name for kin and renamed them separate meals; men read it as an omen of parting.
entries.literal: Emperor Shizu held that guest was not a word for family and changed the name to separate meals; contemporaries took this as an image of separation.

entries.zh: 少時，上晏駕。
entries.en: Not long after, the emperor died.
entries.literal: Before long the emperor died.

entries.zh: 延興元年，海陵王初立，文惠太子冢上有物如人，長數丈，青色，直上天，有聲如雷。
entries.en: Yanxing 1, when the Prince of Hailing was first raised to the throne, above Crown Prince Wenhui’s mound a figure like a man, several zhang in height and green in color, rose straight to Heaven with a roar like thunder.
entries.literal: Yanxing year 1, when the Prince of Hailing was first enthroned, above Crown Prince Wenhui’s tomb something like a person, several zhang tall and green, shot straight to Heaven with a sound like thunder.

entries.zh: 文惠太子在東宮，作「兩頭纖纖」詩，後句云「磊磊落落玉山崩」，自此長王宰相相繼薨徂，二宮晏駕。
entries.en: Crown Prince Wenhui in the Eastern Palace wrote "Two Ends, Fine and Fine"; its last line was "jade mountains crumble, stone on stone"—after that great princes and chief ministers fell one after another, and both palaces buried their lords.
entries.literal: Crown Prince Wenhui in the Eastern Palace composed the poem "Two Ends, Fine and Fine"; the closing line ran "jade mountains topple, heap on heap"—from then on senior princes and chief ministers died in succession, and both palaces saw the emperor die.

entries.zh: 文惠太子作七言詩，後句輒云「愁和諦」。
entries.en: Wenhui wrote seven-character verses whose last line always ended "sorrow—and the Harmonious Emperor."
entries.literal: Crown Prince Wenhui composed seven-character poems; the closing line always ran "grief and the Emperor of Harmony."

entries.zh: 後果有和帝禪位。
entries.en: In time Emperor He did yield the throne.
entries.literal: Later there truly was Emperor He abdicating the throne.

entries.zh: 文惠太子起東田，時人反云「後必有癲童。」
entries.en: Crown Prince Wenhui laid out the Eastern Fields; wits read the name backward and said "after this a frenzied child."
entries.literal: Crown Prince Wenhui built the Eastern Fields; people reversed the name and said "afterward there will surely be a mad child."

entries.zh: 果由太孫失位。
entries.en: So it was when the heir lost his seat.
entries.literal: It came about through the heir apparent losing his place.

entries.zh: 建武四年，王晏子德元所居帷屏，無故有血灑之，少日而散。
entries.en: Jianwu year 4: at the screens in the home of Wang Yan's son Deyuan, blood appeared from nowhere and faded within days.
entries.literal: In Jianwu year 4, at the curtain screens of the residence of Wang Yan's son Deyuan, blood was splashed without cause; in a few days it dispersed.

entries.zh: 晏尋被誅。
entries.en: Soon after, Yan was executed.
entries.literal: Before long Yan was executed.

entries.zh: 建元二年夏，廬陵石陽縣長溪水沖激山麓崩，長六七丈，下得柱千餘口，皆十圍，長者一丈，短者八九尺，頭題有古文字，不可識。
entries.en: In the second year of Jianyuan, summer: in Shiyang, Luling, the Chang stream scoured the mountain foot until six or seven zhang fell away; beneath lay a thousand-odd pillars, each ten arm-spans thick, from one zhang down to eight or nine chi, their heads carved with ancient script no one could read.
entries.literal: the second year of Jianyuan, summer — at Shiyang county in Luling the Chang stream undercut the mountain foot and it collapsed six or seven zhang; below came more than a thousand pillar-sections, all ten arm-spans around, the longest one zhang and the shortest eight or nine chi; the capitals bore ancient characters that could not be read.

entries.zh: 江淹以問王儉，儉云：「江東不閑隸書，此秦漢時柱也。」
entries.en: Jiang Yan consulted Wang Jian, who said: "East of the Yangtze they no longer read clerical script — these are Qin-Han pillars."
entries.literal: Jiang Yan asked Wang Jian; Jian said: "East of the River does not use clerical script; these are pillars from Qin and Han times."

entries.zh: 後年宮車晏駕，世變之象也。
entries.en: In a later year, the emperor died — an omen that the world was changing.
entries.literal: In a later year, the imperial carriage came to rest — a sign that the age was changing.

entries.zh: 建武四年，王晏出至草市，馬驚走，鼓步從車而歸，十餘日，晏誅。
entries.en: Jianwu 4: Wang Yan rode out to Grass Market; his horse panicked and fled; drummers and runners chased the carriage home — within a fortnight Yan was put to death.
entries.literal: Jianwu year 4, Wang Yan went out to Grass Market; his horse bolted; drummers and runners followed the carriage back — within ten-odd days Yan was executed.

entries.zh: 永明元年元日，有小人發白虎樽，旣醉，與筆札，不知所道，直云「憶高帝」。
entries.en: Yongming 1, New Year's Day: a commoner broached the White Tiger wine jar; drunk, he seized brush and paper and scrawled nonsense—over and over only "I remember the Founding Emperor."
entries.literal: On New Year's Day of Yongming year 1, a petty man opened the White Tiger wine jar; drunk, he took brush and paper and wrote without knowing what—only kept saying "remembering the Founding Emperor."

entries.zh: 敕原其罪。
entries.en: An edict pardoned him.
entries.literal: An edict pardoned his crime.

entries.zh: 宋昇明二年，飆風起建康縣南塘里，吹帛一匹入雲，風止，下御路。
entries.en: Song Shengming 2: a whirlwind in Nantang hamlet, Jiankang county, lifted a bolt of cloth into the sky; when the wind died it fell on the Imperial Way.
entries.literal: Song Shengming year 2, a whirlwind rose in Nantang village of Jiankang county and blew a bolt of cloth into the clouds; when the wind stopped it came down on the Imperial Way.

entries.zh: 紀僧真啓太祖當宋氏禪者，其有匹夫居之。
entries.en: Ji Sengzhen told Emperor Taizu that the Song mandate was his—and that a common man would dwell on the omen.
entries.literal: Ji Sengzhen reported to Emperor Taizu that he would receive the Song abdication—a common man would possess it.

entries.zh: 南齊書卷十九‧志第十一
entries.en: Book of the Southern Qi, Volume 19 — Treatise 11
entries.literal: Book of the Southern Qi, Volume 19 — Treatise 11

entries.zh: 后少家貧，勤織作，家人矜其勞，或止之，后終不改。
entries.en: The family was poor in her girlhood, and she wove and worked without rest. Relatives pitied her toil and tried to make her stop; she never changed her ways.
entries.literal: In youth the empress's family was poor; she diligently wove and worked. Her kin took pity on her labor and sometimes tried to stop her, but the empress never changed.

entries.zh: 嫁于宣帝，庶生衡陽元王道度、始安貞王道生，后生太祖。
entries.en: She married Emperor Xuan. By concubines he already had Prince Daodu of Hengyang and Prince Daosheng of Shi'an; afterward she bore Xiao Daocheng, the Grand Ancestor.
entries.literal: She married Emperor Xuan; Prince Daodu of Hengyang and Prince Daosheng of Shi'an were secondary-born (by concubines); afterward she bore the Grand Ancestor.

entries.zh: 太祖年二歲，乳人乏乳，后夢人以兩甌麻粥與之，覺而乳大出，異而說之。
entries.en: When Xiao Daocheng was two, his wet nurse could not supply enough milk. The empress dreamed that someone handed her two bowls of hemp porridge; she awoke to find her milk abundant, and she wondered at the omen.
entries.literal: When the Grand Ancestor was two years old, his wet nurse had insufficient milk. The empress dreamed that someone gave her two bowls of hemp porridge; when she awoke her milk flowed freely—she marveled and spoke of it.

entries.zh: 宣帝從任在外，后常留家治事教子孫。
entries.en: Emperor Xuan was posted away from home while the empress stayed behind to run the household and instruct the children and grandchildren.
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan was away on assignment; the empress often remained at home to manage affairs and teach the children and grandchildren.

entries.zh: 有相者謂后曰：「夫人有貴子而不見也。」
entries.en: A physiognomist told the empress, "My lady has a son of great rank, yet I have not laid eyes on him."
entries.literal: A physiognomist told the empress: "My lady has an eminent son, but I have not seen him."

entries.zh: 后歎曰：「我三兒誰當應之。」
entries.en: She sighed. "I have three sons—which of them can it be?"
entries.literal: The empress sighed and said: "Which of my three sons should it be?"

entries.zh: 呼太祖小字曰：「正應是汝耳。」
entries.en: She called the Grand Ancestor by his childhood name and said, "It must be you."
entries.literal: She called the Grand Ancestor by his childhood name and said: "It must be you after all."

entries.zh: 宣帝殂後，后親自執勤，婢使有過誤，恕不問也。
entries.en: After Emperor Xuan's death she herself saw to the work of the household; when maidservants blundered, she pardoned them without question.
entries.literal: After Emperor Xuan died, the empress personally took charge of labor; when maidservants erred, she forgave them and did not inquire.

entries.zh: 太祖雖從官，而家業本貧，爲建康令時，高宗等冬月猶無縑纊，而奉膳甚厚，后每撤去兼肉，曰：「於我過足矣。」
entries.en: Though Xiao Daocheng held office, the family had always been poor. When he was magistrate of Jiankang, Gaozong and the others still went without padded silk in winter, while the food sent in was lavish—the empress would remove the extra meat and say, "For me this is already too much."
entries.literal: Though the Grand Ancestor held office, the family estate was originally poor; when he was magistrate of Jiankang, Gaozong and the others in winter still lacked silk padding, yet the meals sent were very rich—the empress each time removed the extra meat and said: "For me this is more than enough."

entries.zh: 殂于縣舍，年七十三。
entries.en: She died in the magistrate's quarters, aged seventy-three.
entries.literal: She died at the magistrate's quarters, age seventy-three.

entries.zh: 昇明三年，追贈竟陵公國太夫人，蜜印，畫青綬，祠以太牢。
entries.en: In Shengming year 3 she was posthumously enfeoffed Grand Lady of the Duke of Jingling's state, with honey seal and painted green cord, and honored with the great offering.
entries.literal: Shengming year 3: posthumous enfeoffment as Grand Lady of the state of the Duke of Jingling, with honey seal and painted green cord; sacrifice with the great offering.

entries.zh: 建元元年，追尊孝皇后。
entries.en: In the first year of Jianyuan she was posthumously honored as Empress Xiao.
entries.literal: the first year of Jianyuan: posthumous elevation as Empress Xiao.

entries.zh: 贈外祖父肇之金紫光祿大夫，諡曰敬侯。
entries.en: His maternal grandfather Chen Zhaozhi was made household minister with the purple-gold seal and posthumously titled Marquis Jing.
entries.literal: Her maternal grandfather Zhao was given the post of household minister with the purple-gold seal and posthumous title Marquis Jing.

entries.zh: 后母胡氏為永昌縣靖君。
entries.en: Her mother, née Hu, was made Village Lady Jing of Yongchang county.
entries.literal: The empress's mother, the Hu clan, was made Village Lady Jing of Yongchang county.

entries.zh: 后母桓氏夢吞玉勝生后，時有紫光滿室，以告壽之，壽之曰：「恨非是男。」
entries.en: The empress's mother, née Huan, dreamed she swallowed a jade ornament when bearing her; purple light filled the room. She told Liu Shouzhi, who said, "I regret it was not a boy."
entries.literal: The empress's mother, the Huan clan, dreamed she swallowed a jade hair ornament when bearing the empress; at that time purple light filled the room. She told Liu Shouzhi, and Shouzhi said, "I regret it was not a boy."

entries.zh: 桓曰：「雖女，亦足興家矣。」
entries.en: Huan replied, "Though a girl, she is enough to raise the family."
entries.literal: Huan said, "Though a girl, she is enough to raise the family."

entries.zh: 后每寢臥，家人常見上如有雲氣焉。
entries.en: Whenever she slept, her family often saw cloudlike vapor above her.
entries.literal: Whenever the empress slept, her family often saw above her something like cloud vapor.

entries.zh: 年十餘歲，歸太祖，嚴正有禮法，家庭肅然。
entries.en: In her teens she entered the Grand Ancestor's household; stern, correct, and observant of ritual, she kept the family in awe.
entries.literal: In her teens she went to the Grand Ancestor's household; stern, correct, and observant of ritual, the family was awed into order.

entries.zh: 宋泰豫元年殂，年五十。
entries.en: In the first year of Taiyu of Song she died, aged fifty.
entries.literal: In the first year of Taiyu of Song she died, aged fifty.

entries.zh: 歸葬宣帝墓側，今泰安陵也。
entries.en: She was buried beside Emperor Xuan's tomb, at what is now Taian Mausoleum.
entries.literal: She was buried beside Emperor Xuan's tomb—what is now Taian Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 門生王清與墓工始下鍤，有白兔跳起，尋之不得，及墳成，兔還栖其上。
entries.en: When her student Wang Qing and the grave workers first dug, a white hare leaped up; they searched in vain, and when the mound was finished the hare returned to nest on it.
entries.literal: When her student Wang Qing and the grave workers first struck the spade, a white hare leaped up; they searched but could not find it, and when the mound was finished the hare returned and nested upon it.

entries.zh: 昇明二年，贈竟陵公國夫人。
entries.en: In Shengming year 2 she was posthumously made Lady of the Duke of Jingling's state.
entries.literal: In the second year of Shengming she was posthumously given the title Lady of the Duke of Jingling's state.

entries.zh: 三年，贈齊國妃，印綬如太妃。
entries.en: In year 3 she was made princess consort of Qi, with seals and cords like a grand consort.
entries.literal: In the third year she was made Princess Consort of Qi, with seals and cords like a grand consort.

entries.zh: 建元元年，尊諡昭皇后。
entries.en: In the first year of Jianyuan she was posthumously honored as Empress Zhao.
entries.literal: In the first year of Jianyuan she was honored with the posthumous title Empress Zhao.

entries.zh: 三年，贈后父金紫光祿大夫，母桓氏上〔虞〕都鄉君；
entries.en: In year 3 her father was made household minister with the purple-gold seal, and her mother, née Huan, Chief Village Lady of Duxiang in Shangyu;
entries.literal: In the third year her father was given the post of household minister with the purple-gold seal; her mother, the Huan clan, was made Chief Village Lady of Duxiang in Shangyu;

entries.zh: 壽之子興道司徒屬，文蔚豫章內史，義徽光祿大夫，義倫通直郎。
entries.en: Shouzhi's sons Xingdao, clerk of the minister of works; Wenwei, interior secretary of Yuzhang; Yihui, household minister; and Yilun, regular attendant in the transmission office.
entries.literal: Shouzhi's sons Xingdao, a clerk of the minister of works, Wenwei, interior secretary of Yuzhang, Yihui, household minister, and Yilun, attendant who transmits straight.

entries.zh: 后少與豫章王妃庾氏為娣姒，庾氏勤女工，奉事太祖、昭后恭謹不倦，后不能及，故不為舅姑所重，世祖家好亦薄焉。
entries.en: In youth she was sisters-in-law with Lady Yu, consort of the Prince of Yuzhang; Yu worked diligently at women's crafts and served the Grand Ancestor and Empress Zhao with tireless reverence. The empress could not match her, so her husband's parents did not value her, and Shizong's regard for the household was slight as well.
entries.literal: In youth the empress was sisters-in-law with Lady Yu of the Prince of Yuzhang; Yu diligently practiced women's crafts and served the Grand Ancestor and Empress Zhao with tireless reverence—the empress could not match her, so she was not valued by her husband's parents, and Shizong's regard for the household was likewise slight.

entries.zh: 性剛嚴，竟陵王子良妃袁氏布衣時有過，后加訓罰。
entries.en: She was stern and strict by nature; when Yuan, consort of Prince of Jingling Ziliang, blundered while still a commoner, the empress rebuked and punished her.
entries.literal: By nature stern and strict; when Yuan, consort of Prince of Jingling Ziliang, erred while still a commoner, the empress added reproof and punishment.

entries.zh: 昇明三年，為齊世子妃。
entries.en: In Shengming year 3 she became consort to the Qi heir apparent.
entries.literal: In the third year of Shengming she became consort to the Qi heir apparent.

entries.zh: 建元元年，為皇太子妃。
entries.en: In the first year of Jianyuan she became consort to the crown prince.
entries.literal: In the first year of Jianyuan she became consort to the crown prince.

entries.zh: 三年，后薨。
entries.en: In year 3 the empress died.
entries.literal: In the third year the empress died.

entries.zh: 諡穆妃，葬休安陵。
entries.en: She was posthumously titled Consort Mu and buried at Xiu'an Mausoleum.
entries.literal: She was given the posthumous title Consort Mu and buried at Xiu'an Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 世祖即位，追尊皇后。
entries.en: When Shizong acceded she was posthumously honored as empress.
entries.literal: When Shizong took the throne she was posthumously honored as empress.

entries.zh: 贈璣之金紫光祿大夫，后母檀氏餘杭廣昌鄉元君。
entries.en: Pei Jizhi was made household minister with the purple-gold seal, and the empress's mother, née Tan, Village Lady of Guangchang in Yuhang.
entries.literal: Jizhi was given the post of household minister with the purple-gold seal; the empress's mother, the Tan clan, was made Village Lady of Guangchang in Yuhang.

entries.zh: 宋世，太祖為文惠太子納后，桂陽賊至，太祖在新亭，傳言已沒，宅復為人所抄掠，文惠太子、竟陵王子良奉穆后、庾妃及后挺身送后兄昺之家，事平乃出。
entries.en: In the Song era the Grand Ancestor took her in marriage for Crown Prince Wenhui. When the Guiyang rebels came, the Grand Ancestor was at Xinting; rumor said he had perished, and the residence was plundered again. Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince of Jingling Ziliang, escorting Empress Mu, Lady Yu, and the empress, risked themselves to take them to the empress's brother Bing's house; when order was restored they came out.
entries.literal: In the Song age the Grand Ancestor received the empress in marriage for Crown Prince Wenhui. When the Guiyang rebels arrived, the Grand Ancestor was at Xinting; rumor spread that he had perished, and the residence was again plundered. Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince of Jingling Ziliang, escorting Empress Mu, Lady Yu, and the empress, braved danger to deliver them to the empress's brother Bing's house; when the affair was settled they emerged.

entries.zh: 建元元年，為南郡王妃。
entries.en: In the first year of Jianyuan she became consort to the Prince of Nan commandery.
entries.literal: In the first year of Jianyuan she became consort to the Prince of Nan commandery.

entries.zh: 四年，為皇太子妃，無寵。
entries.en: In year 4 she became consort to the crown prince, without favor.
entries.literal: In the fourth year she became consort to the crown prince, without favor.

entries.zh: 太子為宮人製新麗衣裳及首飾，而后牀帷陳設故舊，釵鑷十餘枚。
entries.en: The crown prince had new splendid garments and ornaments made for palace women, while the empress's bed curtains and furnishings stayed old, with only a dozen or so hairpins and tweezers.
entries.literal: The crown prince had new splendid garments and hair ornaments made for palace women, while the empress's bed curtains and furnishings remained old, with a dozen or so hairpins and tweezers.

entries.zh: 永明十一年，為皇太孫太妃。
entries.en: In Yongming year 11 she became grand consort to the imperial grandson's heir.
entries.literal: In the eleventh year of Yongming she became grand consort to the imperial grandson's heir.

entries.zh: 鬱林即位，尊為皇太后，稱宣德宮。
entries.en: When Yulin acceded she was honored as empress dowager, styled Xuande Palace.
entries.literal: When Yulin took the throne she was honored as empress dowager, styled Xuande Palace.

entries.zh: 贈后父金紫光祿大夫，母桓氏豐安縣君。
entries.en: Her father was made household minister with the purple-gold seal, and her mother, née Huan, County Lady of Feng'an.
entries.literal: Her father was given the post of household minister with the purple-gold seal; her mother, the Huan clan, was made County Lady of Feng'an.

entries.zh: 其年十二月，備法駕謁太廟。
entries.en: That year, in the twelfth month, with full imperial equipage she visited the Great Temple.
entries.literal: That year, in the twelfth month, with full imperial equipage she paid homage at the Great Temple.

entries.zh: 高宗即位，出居鄱陽王故第，為宣德宮。
entries.en: When Gaozong acceded she moved to the former residence of the Prince of Poyang, styled Xuande Palace.
entries.literal: When Gaozong took the throne she moved out to the former residence of the Prince of Poyang, styled Xuande Palace.

entries.zh: 永元三年，梁王定京邑，迎后入宮稱制，至禪位。
entries.en: In Yongyuan year 3 the Prince of Liang secured the capital, welcomed the empress into the palace to rule in regency, and held power until the abdication.
entries.literal: In the third year of Yongyuan the Prince of Liang secured the capital; he welcomed the empress into the palace to hold regency, until the abdication of the throne.

entries.zh: 天監十一年，薨，年五十八。
entries.en: In Tianjian year 11 she died, aged fifty-eight.
entries.literal: In the eleventh year of Tianjian she died, aged fifty-eight.

entries.zh: 葬崇安陵。
entries.en: She was buried at Chong'an Mausoleum.
entries.literal: She was buried at Chong'an Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 諡曰安后。
entries.en: She was posthumously titled Empress An.
entries.literal: Her posthumous title was Empress An.

entries.zh: 兄晃義興太守。
entries.en: Her elder brother Huang was administrator of Yixing.
entries.literal: Her older brother Huang was administrator of Yixing.

entries.zh: 鬱林王何妃名婧英，廬江灊人，撫軍將軍戢之女也。
entries.en: Consort He Jingying of Prince Yulin came from Qian in Lujiang commandery and was the daughter of General Who Pacifies the Army He Ji.
entries.literal: Consort He of Prince Yulin, personal name Jingying, was a native of Qian in Lujiang and the daughter of General Who Pacifies the Army He Ji.

entries.zh: 永明二年，納爲南郡王妃。
entries.en: In Yongming year 2 she entered the household as consort to the Prince of Nan commandery.
entries.literal: Yongming year 2: she was received as consort to the Prince of Nan commandery.

entries.zh: 十一年，爲皇太孫妃。
entries.en: In year 11 she became consort to the heir apparent of the imperial grandson.
entries.literal: Year 11: she became consort to the heir apparent of the imperial grandson.

entries.zh: 鬱林王卽位，爲皇后。
entries.en: When Prince Yulin acceded, she was made empress.
entries.literal: When Prince Yulin took the throne, she became empress.

entries.zh: 嫡母劉氏爲高昌縣都鄉君，所生母宋氏，爲餘杭廣昌鄉君。
entries.en: Her foster mother, née Liu, was made Chief Village Lady of Duxiang in Gaochang county; her birth mother, née Song, Village Lady of Guangchang in Yuhang.
entries.literal: Her formal mother, the Liu clan, was made Chief Village Lady of Duxiang in Gaochang county; her birth mother, the Song clan, Village Lady of Guangchang in Yuhang.

entries.zh: 將拜，鏡在牀無故墮地。
entries.en: On the eve of her investiture a mirror on the bed fell to the floor without cause.
entries.literal: As the investiture approached, a mirror on the bed fell to the floor for no reason.

entries.zh: 其冬，與太后同日謁太廟。
entries.en: That winter she and the empress dowager visited the Great Temple on the same day.
entries.literal: That winter she and the empress dowager on the same day paid homage at the Great Temple.

entries.zh: 明敬劉皇后諱惠端，彭城人，光祿大夫道弘孫也。
entries.en: Empress Mingjing Liu, whose personal name was Huiduan, came from Pengcheng and was the granddaughter of Household Minister Liu Daohong.
entries.literal: Empress Mingjing Liu, personal name Huiduan, was a native of Pengcheng and granddaughter of Household Minister Daohong.

entries.zh: 太祖爲高宗納之。
entries.en: The Grand Progenitor arranged her marriage to Gaozong.
entries.literal: The Grand Progenitor secured her in marriage for Gaozong.

entries.zh: 建元三年，除西昌侯夫人。
entries.en: In the third year of Jianyuan she was made lady to the marquis of Xichang.
entries.literal: In the third year of Jianyuan she was invested as Lady of the Marquis of Xichang.

entries.zh: 永明七年，卒，葬江乘縣張山。
entries.en: In the seventh year of Yongming she died and was buried at Zhang Mountain in Jiangcheng county.
entries.literal: In the seventh year of Yongming she died and was buried at Zhang Mountain in Jiangcheng county.

entries.zh: 延興元年，贈宣城王妃。
entries.en: In the first year of Yanxing she was posthumously titled princess consort of Xuancheng.
entries.literal: In the first year of Yanxing she was posthumously given the title Princess Consort of Xuancheng.

entries.zh: 高宗卽位，追尊爲敬皇后。
entries.en: When Gaozong acceded, she was posthumously honored as Empress Jing.
entries.literal: When Gaozong took the throne, she was posthumously honored as Empress Jing.

entries.zh: 贈父通直郎景猷金紫光祿大夫，母王氏平陽鄉君。
entries.en: Her father Jingyou, a regular attendant in the transmission office, was posthumously made household minister with the golden seal and purple cord; her mother, Lady Wang, was made lady of Pingyang township.
entries.literal: Her father Jingyou, General of Transmission who was Regular, was posthumously made Household Minister with the Golden Seal and Purple Cord; her mother, Lady Wang, was made Lady of Pingyang township.

entries.zh: 永泰元年，高宗崩，改葬，祔于興安陵。
entries.en: In the first year of Yongtai, when Gaozong died, she was reinterred and laid beside him in Xing'an Mausoleum.
entries.literal: In the first year of Yongtai, when Gaozong died, she was reburied and consigned to Xing'an Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：后妃之德，著自風謠，義起閨房，而道化天下。
entries.en: The historian writes: The virtue of empresses and consorts shines in folk song; their righteousness begins behind closed doors and spreads until it reshapes the world.
entries.literal: The historian writes: The virtue of empresses and consorts is recorded in folk song; righteousness rises in the inner chamber and transforms the realm beneath Heaven.

entries.zh: 繰盆獻種，罔非耕織，佩管晨興，與子同事，可以光熙閫業，作儷公侯。
entries.en: They reel the cocoon basin and offer seed—nothing but spinning and weaving; they gird the reed and rise at dawn, working beside their sons—thus the inner household glows and they stand as equals to dukes and marquises.
entries.literal: Reeling the cocoon-tray and offering seed—all is spinning and weaving; girding the shuttle-gauge and rising at dawn, sharing toil with their sons—they can brighten the household estate and stand as peers to dukes and marquises.

entries.zh: 孝、昭二后，竝有賢明之訓，不得母臨萬國。
entries.en: The Xiao and Gao empresses both bore wise instruction, yet never ruled the realm as mothers of the state.
entries.literal: Empresses Xiao and Gao both possessed wise and clarifying instruction, yet could not mother the myriad domains.

entries.zh: 寶命方昌，椒庭虛位，有婦人焉，空慕周興，禎符顯瑞，徒萃徽名。
entries.en: While the sacred mandate was rising, the empress's courts stood vacant; some women only dreamed of a Zhou restoration—bright omens and lucky signs heaped up nothing but hollow fame.
entries.literal: While the precious mandate flourished anew, the pepper courts stood empty; certain women only yearned in vain for the Zhou revival—auspicious tokens and bright omens gathered nothing but empty glory.

entries.zh: 若使掖作同休，陰教遠燮，則馬、鄧風流，復存乎此。
entries.en: Had the side palaces rested in one accord and the women's teaching steadied the realm from within, the elegance of the Ma and Deng empresses might have returned here.
entries.literal: Had the lateral palaces shared one repose and the inner teaching harmonized the realm from afar, the grace of Ma and Deng might have lived here again.

entries.zh: 太祖創命，宮禁貶約，毀宋明之紫極，革前代之踰奢，衣不文繡，色無紅采，永巷貧空，有同素室。
entries.en: At the Grand Progenitor's founding, the palace was pared to austerity: he razed Emperor Ming of Song's Purple Ultimate Hall and cut the extravagance of earlier reigns—garments without figured embroidery, colors without red; the long alleys were empty and poor as plain chambers.
entries.literal: When the Grand Progenitor founded the dynasty, palace bounds were stripped back: he destroyed Emperor Ming of Song's Purple Ultimate, reformed past dynasties' excess; robes bore no brocade patterns, colors no scarlet; the long alleys were poor and bare as undecorated rooms.

entries.zh: 世祖嗣位，運藉休平，壽昌前興，鳳華晚搆，香柏文檉，花梁繡柱，雕金鏤寶，頗用房帷，趙瑟吳趨，承閑奏曲，歲費傍恩，足使充牣，事由私蓄，無損國儲。
entries.en: When Shizu succeeded, the age rested on peace—Shouchang rose early, Fenghua late; fragrant cypress and patterned rafters, painted beams and embroidered pillars, carved gold and set gems crowded the curtained halls; Zhao zithers and Wu songs filled idle hours; yearly outlays from side revenues overflowed the vaults—paid from private stores, never touching the state coffers.
entries.literal: When Shizu succeeded, fortune rode on peaceful times—Shouchang built early, Fenghua raised late; fragrant cypress and patterned beams, floral rafters and embroidered pillars, carved gold and inset jewels filled the curtained chambers; Zhao harps and Wu airs were played in leisure; yearly spending from ancillary favor was enough to overflow the stores—all from private hoards, never draining the state treasury.

entries.zh: 高宗仗數矯情，外行儉陋，內奉宮業，曾莫云改。
entries.en: Gaozong trusted omens and played at austerity—plain and mean in public, yet he kept the palace estate as before and never breathed a word of reform.
entries.literal: Gaozong leaned on numerology and feigned restraint: outwardly frugal and plain, inwardly he sustained palace industry and never spoke of change.

entries.zh: 東昏喪道，侈風大扇，銷糜海內，以贍浮飾，哲婦傾城，同符殷、夏。
entries.en: Dong Hun abandoned the Way; luxury blazed across the land; he melted the empire to pay for idle display—wise women toppled cities, in the manner of Yin and Xia.
entries.literal: Dong Hun lost the Way; extravagance swept wide; he melted the realm to feed vain ornament—sagacious women overturned cities, matching Yin and Xia alike.

entries.zh: 嗚呼！
entries.en: Alas!
entries.literal: Alas!

entries.zh: 所以垂戒於方來也。
entries.en: So a warning is set down for ages still to come.
entries.literal: Thus a warning is left to generations yet to come.

entries.zh: 宣孝陳皇后諱道止，臨淮東陽人，魏司徒陳矯後。
entries.en: Empress Xuanxiao Chen Daozhi came from Dongyang in Linhuai commandery and was descended from Chen Jiao, minister of works of Wei.
entries.literal: Empress Xuanxiao of the Chen clan, taboo name Daozhi, was a native of Dongyang in Linhuai and a descendant of Chen Jiao, minister of works of Wei.

entries.zh: 父肇之，郡孝廉。
entries.en: Her father Chen Zhaozhi had been a commandery filial-and-incorrupt nominee.
entries.literal: Her father Chen Zhaozhi was a commandery filial and incorrupt candidate.

entries.zh: 吳郡韓藺英，婦人有文辭。
entries.en: Han Linying of Wu commandery was a woman of literary gifts.
entries.literal: Han Linying of Wu commandery was a woman of literary talent.

entries.zh: 宋孝武世，獻中興賦，被賞入宮。
entries.en: Under Emperor Xiaowu of Song she submitted the "Rhapsody on Restoration" and, rewarded, was admitted to the palace.
entries.literal: In the age of Emperor Xiaowu of Song she presented the "Zhongxing Rhapsody" and, prized, was brought into the palace.

entries.zh: 宋明帝世，用爲宮中職僚。
entries.en: Under Emperor Ming of Song she served on the palace staff.
entries.literal: In the age of Emperor Ming of Song she was employed as a palace staff officer.

entries.zh: 世祖以爲博士，教六宮書學，以其年老多識，呼爲「韓公」。
entries.en: Shizong appointed her erudite to instruct the six palaces in writing and learning; in her great age and wide knowledge they called her "Lord Han."
entries.literal: Shizong made her a erudite to teach the six palaces calligraphy and learning; because she was old and knew much, they called her "Lord Han."

entries.zh: 后稟性淫亂，爲妃時，便與外人姦通。
entries.en: The empress was wanton by nature; even as a princess consort she took lovers from outside the palace.
entries.literal: The empress was by nature licentious; even as a consort she had illicit relations with outsiders.

entries.zh: 在後宮，復通帝左右楊珉之，與同寢處如伉儷。
entries.en: In the inner quarters she took up with Yang Minzhi, a favorite at the emperor's side, and they slept and lived together like husband and wife.
entries.literal: In the inner palace she again had relations with Yang Minzhi, an attendant at the emperor's side, sharing bed and board like man and wife.

entries.zh: 珉之又與帝相愛褻，故帝恣之。
entries.en: Minzhi was likewise intimate with the emperor, and the emperor let them have their way.
entries.literal: Minzhi was also on intimate terms with the emperor, so the emperor indulged them.

entries.zh: 迎后親戚入宮，賞賜人百數十萬。
entries.en: She summoned the empress's kin into the palace and lavished rewards running into hundreds of thousands.
entries.literal: She brought the empress's kinsmen into the palace and bestowed rewards in the hundreds of thousands.

entries.zh: 以世祖耀靈殿處后家屬。
entries.en: Shizu's Yaoling Hall was set aside to lodge the empress's kin.
entries.literal: Shizu's Yaoling Hall was given over to house the empress's family.

entries.zh: 帝被廢，后貶爲王妃。
entries.en: When the emperor was deposed, the empress was reduced to princess consort.
entries.literal: When the emperor was deposed, the empress was demoted to princess consort.

entries.zh: 舊顯陽、昭陽二殿，太后、皇后所居也。
entries.en: The Xianyang and Zhaoyang halls had long been the residences of empress dowager and empress.
entries.literal: Formerly the Xianyang and Zhaoyang halls were where the empress dowager and empress dwelt.

entries.zh: 永明中無太后、皇后，羊貴嬪居昭陽殿西，范貴妃居昭陽殿東，寵姬荀昭華居鳳華柏殿。
entries.en: In the Yongming era there was no empress dowager or empress: Noble Consort Yang lived west of Zhaoyang Hall, Honored Consort Fan to the east, and the favored Xun Zhaohua in the Phoenix Splendor Cypress Hall.
entries.literal: In Yongming there was neither empress dowager nor empress; Noble Consort Yang dwelt west of Zhaoyang Hall, Honored Consort Fan east of Zhaoyang Hall, and the favored lady Xun Zhaohua in the Phoenix Splendor Cypress Hall.

entries.zh: 宮內御所居壽昌畫殿南閣，置白鷺鼓吹二部；
entries.en: In the south gallery of the Shouchang Painted Hall, the emperor's inner quarters, two companies of egret-reed pipes were stationed;
entries.literal: At the south gallery of the Shouchang Painted Hall, where the emperor dwelt within the palace, two companies of egret-reed pipes were installed;

entries.zh: 乾光殿東西頭，置鍾磬兩廂：皆宴樂處也。
entries.en: at the east and west ends of Qianguang Hall, bell and stone galleries on either flank—all were halls for feasting and music.
entries.literal: at the east and west ends of Qianguang Hall, bell and chime galleries on either side: all were places for feasting and music.

entries.zh: 上數遊幸諸苑囿，載宮人從後車，宮內深隱，不聞端門鼓漏聲，置鍾於景陽樓上，宮人聞鍾聲，早起裝飾，至今此鍾唯應五鼓及三鼓也。
entries.en: The emperor often toured the royal parks with palace women in the train behind his carriage. Deep inside the palace the drum and clepsydra at the Duan Gate could not be heard, so a bell was hung on Jingyang Tower. At its stroke the women rose early to dress—to this day it sounds only at the fifth watch and the third.
entries.literal: The emperor often toured the parks and enclosures, carrying palace women in the rear carriage. Deep within the palace one did not hear the drum and water-clock at the Duan Gate; a bell was set on Jingyang Tower. When palace women heard the bell they rose early to dress and adorn themselves—to this day that bell answers only the fifth watch and the third watch.

entries.zh: 車駕數幸琅邪城，宮人常從，早發至湖北埭，雞始鳴。
entries.en: The court often went to Langya walled town, palace women in attendance. They left at first light and reached Hubei landing at the first cockcrow.
entries.literal: The imperial carriage often visited Langya walled town; palace women regularly followed. They set out early and reached Hubei ferry landing when the cock first crowed.

entries.zh: 和帝王皇后名蕣華，琅邪臨沂人，太尉儉孫也。
entries.en: Empress Wang of Emperor He, named Shunhua, came from Linyi in Langya commandery and was the granddaughter of Grand Commandant Wang Jian.
entries.literal: Empress Wang of Emperor He, named Shunhua, was a native of Linyi in Langya and granddaughter of Grand Commandant Jian.

entries.zh: 初爲隨王妃。
entries.en: At first she was princess consort of Sui.
entries.literal: At first she was princess consort of Sui.

entries.zh: 中興元年，爲皇后。
entries.en: In the first year of Zhongxing she was raised to empress.
entries.literal: In the first year of Zhongxing she was made empress.

entries.zh: 帝禪位，后降爲妃。
entries.en: When the emperor yielded the throne, the empress was reduced to consort.
entries.literal: When the emperor abdicated the throne, the empress was demoted to consort.

entries.zh: 南齊書卷二十‧列傳第一
entries.en: Book of the Southern Qi, Volume 20 — Biographies 1
entries.literal: Book of the Southern Qi, Volume 20 — Biographies 1

entries.zh: 文惠太子長懋字雲喬，世祖長子也。
entries.en: Crown Prince Wenhui, Xiao Zhangmao, courtesy name Yunqiao, was the eldest son of Emperor Wu.
entries.literal: Crown Prince Wenhui Zhangmao, courtesy name Yunqiao, was the eldest son of Emperor Wu.

entries.zh: 世祖年未弱冠而生太子，爲太祖所愛。
entries.en: Emperor Wu was not yet twenty when Xiao Zhangmao was born, and Xiao Daocheng, the Grand Ancestor, doted on him.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu had not yet come of age when the crown prince was born, and the Grand Ancestor loved him.

entries.zh: 姿容豐潤，小字白澤。
entries.en: He was handsome and well favored; in childhood he was called Baize.
entries.literal: His bearing was full and fair; his childhood name was Baize.

entries.zh: 宋元徽末，隨世祖在郢。
entries.en: Late in the Yuánhuī era of Song he was with Emperor Wu at Ying.
entries.literal: At the end of the Yuánhuī era of Song, he followed Emperor Wu at Ying.

entries.zh: 世祖還鎮盆城拒沈攸之，使太子勞接將帥，親侍軍旅。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu went back to hold Pencheng against Shen Youzhi, he sent the prince to receive the commanders and share the hardships of the camp.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu returned to garrison at Pencheng to resist Shen Youzhi, he had the crown prince greet the generals and take part in the army in person.

entries.zh: 除秘書郎，不拜。
entries.en: He was named secretary gentleman but declined to take up the post.
entries.literal: He was appointed secretary gentleman but did not accept the office.

entries.zh: 授輔國將軍，遷晉熙王撫軍主簿。
entries.en: He was made General Who Assists the State and moved to be chief clerk on Prince Jinxi's pacifying staff.
entries.literal: He was made General Who Assists the State and transferred to serve as steward to the General Who Pacifies the Army under Prince Jinxi.

entries.zh: 事寧，世祖遣太子還都。
entries.en: After peace was restored, Emperor Wu sent the prince back to the capital.
entries.literal: When the affair was settled, Emperor Wu sent the crown prince back to the capital.

entries.zh: 太祖方創霸業，心存嫡嗣，謂太子曰：「汝還，吾事辦矣。」
entries.en: Xiao Daocheng was then laying the foundations of rule and had the succession at heart. He told the prince, "When you return, my work is finished."
entries.literal: The Grand Ancestor was then founding his hegemony and kept the legitimate heir in mind. He told the crown prince: "When you return, my task is done."

entries.zh: 處之府東齋，令通文武賓客。
entries.en: He quartered him in the east study of the princely residence and opened the doors to guests civil and martial alike.
entries.literal: He lodged him in the east study of the princely residence and allowed him access to civil and military guests.

entries.zh: 敕荀伯玉曰：「我出行日，城中軍悉受長懋節度。
entries.en: He instructed Xun Boyu, "On days when I leave the city, every soldier in the capital shall answer to Zhangmao.
entries.literal: He charged Xun Boyu: "On days when I go out, all troops in the city shall obey Zhangmao's command.

entries.zh: 我雖不行，內外直防及諸門甲兵，悉令長懋時時履行。」
entries.en: Even when I stay in, let Zhangmao walk the inner and outer watches and the armored guards at every gate."
entries.literal: Even when I do not go out, let Zhangmao from time to time inspect all inner and outer guards and the armored men at every gate."

entries.zh: 轉秘書丞，以與宣帝諱同，不就，改除中書郎，遷黃門侍郎，未拜。
entries.en: He was transferred to secretary director, but the title matched the taboo of Emperor Xuan of Jin, so he declined; he was reassigned gentleman of the palace secretariat and promoted gentleman attendant at the yellow gate, without yet taking office.
entries.literal: He was transferred to secretary director, but since that title matched the taboo name of Emperor Xuan of Jin, he did not take it; he was reassigned as gentleman of the palace secretariat and promoted to gentleman attendant at the yellow gate, but had not yet assumed office.

entries.zh: 升明三年，太祖將受禪，世祖已還京師，以襄陽兵馬重鎮，不欲處他族，出太子爲持節、都督雍梁二州、郢州之竟陵、司州之隨郡軍事、左中郎將、寧蠻校尉、雍州刺史。
entries.en: In Shengming year 3, as Xiao Daocheng prepared to accept the throne, Emperor Wu was already in the capital. Xiangyang held the empire's horses and arms, and he would not trust another house with it—so he sent the prince out as bearer of the staff, superintendent of Yong and Liang, of Jingling in Ying and Sui in Si, left central commander, colonel pacifying the barbarians, and inspector of Yong.
entries.literal: In the third year of Shengming, as the Grand Ancestor was about to receive the abdication, Emperor Wu had already returned to the capital. Because Xiangyang was a key stronghold for troops and horses and he did not wish to place another clan in charge, he sent out the crown prince as bearer of the staff, superintendent of military affairs in the two provinces of Yong and Liang, Jingling in Ying province, and Sui commandery in Si province, left central commander, colonel pacifying the barbarians, and inspector of Yong province.

entries.zh: 建元元年，封南郡王，邑二千戶。
entries.en: In the first year of Jianyuan he was enfeoffed Prince of Nan commandery, fief of two thousand households.
entries.literal: In the first year of Jianyuan he was enfeoffed as Prince of Nan commandery, with a fief of two thousand households.

entries.zh: 江左未有嫡皇孫封王，始自此也。
entries.en: South of the Yangtze no legitimate imperial grandson had ever been made a prince before; the precedent began here.
entries.literal: Never before in the lands south of the Yangtze had a legitimate imperial grandson been enfeoffed as prince; it began with this.

entries.zh: 進號征虜將軍。
entries.en: His title was raised to General Who Subdues the Barbarians.
entries.literal: He was advanced in title to General Who Subdues the Barbarians.

entries.zh: 文惠太子
entries.en: Crown Prince Wenhui
entries.literal: Crown Prince Wenhui

entries.zh: 太子素多疾，體又過壯，常在宮內，簡於遨遊。
entries.en: The crown prince had long been sickly, yet his body was overfull; he kept to the inner palace and went little abroad.
entries.literal: The crown prince had long been prone to illness, yet his frame was overly stout; he often stayed within the palace and was sparing in outings.

entries.zh: 玩弄羽儀，多所僭儗，雖咫尺宮禁，而上終不知。
entries.en: He toyed with regalia and overstepped rank in many ways; the palace forbidden zone was only steps away, yet the emperor never learned of it.
entries.literal: He played with insignia of rank and usurped many prerogatives; though the forbidden precinct lay only a few paces away, the emperor never knew.

entries.zh: 十年，豫章王嶷薨，太子見上友于旣至，造碑文奏之，未及鐫勒。
entries.en: In the tenth year the prince of Yuzhang, Xiao Ni, died; seeing the emperor's brotherly love at its fullest, the crown prince drafted an epitaph and submitted it, but it had not yet been cut in stone.
entries.literal: In the tenth year, the Prince of Yuzhang, Xiao Ni, died; the crown prince, seeing the emperor's brotherly affection had reached its height, composed an epitaph and presented it, but it was not yet carved.

entries.zh: 十一年春正月，太子有疾，上自臨視，有憂色。
entries.en: In the first month of spring of the eleventh year the crown prince fell ill; the emperor visited him in person, worry plain on his face.
entries.literal: In the first month of spring in the eleventh year, the crown prince fell ill; the emperor came in person to visit him, his face troubled.

entries.zh: 疾篤，上表曰：「臣地屬元良，業微三善，光道樹風，於焉蓋闕，晨宵忷懼，有若臨淵。
entries.en: As the sickness deepened he memorialized: "I hold the heir's station, yet my fulfillment of the three duties is slight; to brighten the Way and set the tone for the realm—there I have failed; dawn to dusk I tremble as at a cliff's edge.
entries.literal: When the illness turned grave, he submitted a memorial saying: "Your servant stands in the place of the heir, yet my achievement in the three duties is slight; to illumine the Way and plant custom—there I am wanting; morning and night I am anxious, as one standing over an abyss.

entries.zh: 攝生舛和，構離痾疾，大漸惟幾，顧陰待謝。
entries.en: In keeping my health I fell out of balance and brought on this lingering malady; the great change draws near, only a breath remains; I face the shade and wait to go.
entries.literal: In tending my life I lost harmony and drew on myself this wasting illness; the great transition is near, only a little remains; I turn toward shadow and await departure.

entries.zh: 守器難永，視膳長違，仰戀慈顏，內懷感哽。
entries.en: To keep the vessel is not for long; to watch over your meals I must forever forgo; I lift my eyes to your gracious countenance and my throat closes with grief.
entries.literal: To guard the vessel long is hard; to attend your meals will be forever denied; looking up I yearn for your kindly face, and within I choke with grief.

entries.zh: 竊惟死生定分，理不足悲，伏願割無已之悼，損旣往之傷，寶衛聖躬，同休七百，臣雖沒九泉，無所遺恨。」
entries.en: Yet I know life and death are allotted and need not be mourned; I beg you end grief without measure and ease sorrow for what has passed, guard your sacred person, and share fortune for seven hundred years—though I go down to the nine springs, I shall have no regret."
entries.literal: I reflect that life and death are fixed allotments and reason gives no cause for grief; I humbly pray you cut off unending mourning and lessen grief for what is past, treasure and guard your sacred person, share blessing for seven hundred years—even if your servant sinks to the nine springs, no regret will remain."

entries.zh: 時年三十六。
entries.en: He was thirty-six.
entries.literal: He was thirty-six years old.

entries.zh: 太子年始過立，久在儲宮，得參政事；
entries.en: The crown prince had only just come of age for investiture; long resident in the Eastern Palace, he had already shared in affairs of state;
entries.literal: The crown prince had only just passed the age of investiture; long in the Eastern Palace, he had taken part in government affairs;

entries.zh: 內外百司，咸謂旦暮繼體。
entries.en: inside and outside the court, every office assumed he would succeed any day.
entries.literal: within and without, every office held that he would succeed before long.

entries.zh: 及薨，朝野驚惋焉。
entries.en: When he died, court and country were shaken with grief.
entries.literal: When he died, court and country were struck with shock and regret.

entries.zh: 上幸東宮，臨哭盡哀，詔斂以袞冕之服，諡曰文惠，葬崇安陵。
entries.en: The emperor came to the Eastern Palace and mourned with full grief; he ordered the heir enshrouded in full regalia, posthumously titled him Wenhui, and buried him at Chong'an Mausoleum.
entries.literal: The emperor came to the Eastern Palace and wept there with full grief; he ordered him enshrouded in full ceremonial robes, gave the posthumous title Wenhui, and buried him at Chong'an Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 世祖履行東宮，見太子服翫過制，大怒，勑有司隨事毀除，以東田殿堂爲崇虛館。
entries.en: Shizu walked through the Eastern Palace, saw the crown prince's dress and playthings far past statute, and in a rage ordered the offices to demolish them on the spot; the Eastern Fields halls became the Chongxu Lodge.
entries.literal: Shizu inspected the Eastern Palace, saw the crown prince's garments and curios beyond regulation, and in great anger ordered the offices to destroy them as found and made the Eastern Fields halls into the Chongxu Lodge.

entries.zh: 鬱林立，追尊爲文帝，廟稱世宗。
entries.en: When Yulin took the throne, he was posthumously honored as Emperor Wen, with the temple name Shizong.
entries.literal: When Yulin was established, he was posthumously honored as Emperor Wen; his temple title was Shizong.

entries.zh: 會北虜南侵，上慮當出樊、沔。
entries.en: When the northern enemy pushed south, the throne feared it might have to withdraw toward Fan and Mian.
entries.literal: When the northern barbarians invaded south, the emperor feared the court might have to move out toward Fan and Mian.

entries.zh: 二年，征爲侍中、中軍將軍，置府，鎮石頭。
entries.en: In year 2 he was recalled as palace attendant and general of the central army, given a staff, and posted to Stone City.
entries.literal: In year 2 he was summoned as palace attendant and general of the central army, with a staff established, and garrisoned at Stone City.

entries.zh: 穆妃薨，成服日，車駕出臨喪，朝議疑太子應出門迎。
entries.en: When Consort Mu died, on the day he finished putting on mourning the emperor rode out in person. The court debated whether the prince should go out to meet the carriage.
entries.literal: When Consort Mu died, on the day of completing mourning dress the imperial carriage went out to condole. Court discussion was divided on whether the crown prince should go out to welcome it.

entries.zh: 左僕射王儉曰：「尋《禮記‧服問》『君所主夫人妻、太子、嫡婦』，言國君爲此三人爲主喪也。
entries.en: Wang Jian, left vice minister, said, "The Book of Rites, 'Dress Questions,' says the lord himself presides for his wife, the heir apparent's wife, and the chief daughter-in-law—that is, the sovereign leads mourning for these three.
entries.literal: Left vice minister Wang Jian said: "If we look to 'Dress Questions' in the Book of Rites—'for the lord's wife, the heir apparent's wife, and the chief daughter-in-law, the lord himself presides over mourning'—that means the sovereign presides over mourning for these three.

entries.zh: 今鸞輿臨降，自以主喪而至，雖因事撫慰，義不在吊，南郡以下不應出門奉迎。
entries.en: Today the imperial carriage comes down as chief mourner. Comfort may be offered on the way, but the visit is not a condolence call; the Prince of Nan and his household should not go out to welcome it.
entries.literal: Now the imperial phoenix carriage descends; it comes in its capacity as chief mourner. Though there is incidental consolation, the rite is not one of condolence; the Prince of Nan commandery and those below him should not go out to welcome it.

entries.zh: 但尊極所臨，禮有變革，權去杖絰，移立戶外，足表情敬，無煩止哭。
entries.en: Yet when the supreme presence arrives, ritual bends: lay aside staff and sackcloth for the moment and stand outside the door—reverence enough without forcing an end to weeping.
entries.literal: Yet where the supreme honor arrives, ritual may bend: for the moment put aside staff and hemp, and stand outside the door—enough to show reverence without requiring one to cease weeping.

entries.zh: 皇太子旣一宮之主，自應以車駕幸宮，依常奉候。
entries.en: The heir apparent is master of his own palace; when the carriage honors his quarters he should receive it in the usual way.
